title: AI Agents and Tool Use
brief: AI agents go beyond chatting by planning steps, running software tools, and reacting to real results. Let's test how they work, where they shine, and how they fail.

questions.question: What makes an AI agent different from a plain chatbot that only replies to your message?
questions.answer: An agent runs in a loop instead of giving one single reply. It plans a step, calls external tools, reads the result, and picks the next action. It keeps repeating that cycle until it finishes the goal or gets stuck.
key_points: It loops by calling tools, reading results, and deciding its own next step
It keeps repeating that cycle until the task is complete
A plain chatbot stops after one single text reply
questions.hint: Picture a chef tasting the soup, adding salt, and checking again rather than serving the very first pour.
questions.fun_fact: Anthropic found that many top coding agents skip heavy frameworks and run on a simple loop with just a few well-designed tools.

questions.question: When an AI agent uses a tool like a calculator or web search, what actually happens under the hood?
questions.answer: The language model never runs the tool directly because it only outputs text. Instead, it writes a structured request naming the tool and its inputs. The surrounding program runs that code and hands the output back to the model.
key_points: The language model outputs a structured request with the tool name and arguments
The host program runs the tool and sends the result back to the model
The model itself only produces text and cannot run external code directly
questions.hint: Think of a brain in a jar that must ask a helper outside to press buttons and read the screen.
questions.fun_fact: Because tool calls are still just generated text, a model can invent fake tool names unless the host app checks every request.

questions.question: How does the ReAct pattern pair thinking with acting, and why does each side need the other?
questions.answer: ReAct alternates between a short written thought, a tool action, and the returned observation. Reasoning helps the agent break down goals, track progress, and recover when an action fails. Acting brings in fresh outside facts, which stops pure reasoning from drifting into made-up claims.
key_points: It repeats a thought, an action, and an observation step by step
Written thoughts help the agent plan, adjust, or recover from errors
Actions bring in real external facts so reasoning stays grounded instead of guessing
questions.hint: Imagine a detective jotting notes on a board after each clue before choosing which lead to chase.
questions.fun_fact: The original ReAct paper tested the same simple loop on both Wikipedia fact-finding and text-based household puzzle games.

questions.question: How does retrieval-augmented generation give an agent new knowledge without retraining, and why can it still hallucinate?
questions.answer: First, the system searches an outside document store for passages that match the question. It pastes those retrieved passages straight into the prompt so the model answers from fresh text. Hallucinations still happen when search pulls the wrong snippet or the model ignores the source text.
key_points: It searches external documents and inserts matching passages into the prompt at answer time
It can still hallucinate if retrieval fetches wrong or outdated snippets, or if the model ignores or misreads the retrieved text
Because documents live outside the model weights, you can update facts without retraining
questions.hint: Compare it to an open-book exam where a student can flip to a bad page or skim past a line.
questions.fun_fact: Researchers invented retrieval-augmented generation years before modern chatbots arrived by connecting an early text model to a searchable Wikipedia index.

questions.question: Why does an agent get worse as tool outputs fill its context window, and how does external memory help?
questions.answer: As raw tool outputs pile up, the model spreads its attention thin and suffers context rot. Important instructions get buried in noise, so recall drops long before the token limit hits. External memory stores notes outside the active window and fetches only relevant pieces when needed.
key_points: Piling up noisy tool outputs spreads the model's attention thin, buries key instructions, or hurts recall
External memory stores information outside the active prompt and loads only relevant pieces when needed
Teams also fight bloat by summarizing past turns or dropping bulky raw logs
questions.hint: Consider working at a messy desk covered in receipts versus using a neat filing cabinet across the room.
questions.fun_fact: Some agent systems spin up fresh helper sub-agents with blank context windows so noisy web searches never clutter the main agent's workspace.

questions.question: How does indirect prompt injection hijack an agent's tools, and why do teams sandbox it with least privilege?
questions.answer: An attacker hides sneaky commands inside untrusted data like a webpage, email, or file. Because the model blends data and instructions together, it can obey that trap and misuse its tools. Sandboxing with least privilege limits access, so a hijacked agent cannot leak secrets or wipe data.
key_points: Hidden instructions placed inside untrusted external data trick the model into running unauthorized tool actions
Sandboxing and least privilege restrict permissions so a hijacked agent can only cause limited harm
Language models struggle to strictly separate trusted system rules from untrusted text they read
questions.hint: Suppose a bank courier opens a letter containing a forged note ordering them to empty the vault, so you only hand them a small cash box.
questions.fun_fact: Security researchers showed that poisoned prompts can spread like computer worms by tricking an email assistant into forwarding the same trap to new victims.

questions.question: Why does an agent that gets almost every single step right still fail often on a twenty-step task?
questions.answer: Small error rates multiply across steps, so a 90 percent step score fails most twenty-step runs. One early mistake also poisons later decisions because the agent builds on its own bad output. Without clear checks or stop rules, agents also burn tokens repeating the same broken retry loop.
key_points: Small per-step errors compound across long chains, so even high step accuracy yields low overall success
One early error can cascade into later steps or trap the agent in a stuck retry loop
Checkpoints, verification steps, and turn limits help stop errors from snowballing
questions.hint: Try rolling dice a dozen times when you only win if you dodge snake eyes on every throw.
questions.fun_fact: Even an agent that nails 95 percent of individual steps clears a twenty-step chain just over one third of the time.

questions.question: When should you choose a fixed workflow over an autonomous agent, and what do you gain by doing that?
questions.answer: Pick a fixed workflow whenever the task steps are clear and predictable up front. Scripted paths run faster, cost less, and are far easier to test and debug. Save open-ended agents for messy problems where you cannot map out the steps ahead of time.
key_points: Use a fixed workflow when the task steps are known and predictable up front
Fixed workflows bring better reliability, lower cost, lower latency, or easier debugging than autonomous loops
Save autonomous agents for open-ended problems where the needed steps cannot be mapped in advance
questions.hint: Contrast a train gliding along steel rails with an off-road truck exploring unmarked trails.
questions.fun_fact: Anthropic's own agent guide tells engineers to skip autonomous agents first and see if a plain prompt or scripted pipeline already solves the job.
